page: Amazon Web Services c8gd.8xlarge is a compute-optimized server powered by 32 dedicated physical cores of the ARM64 AWS Graviton Neoverse-V2 processor, operating at 2.8 GHz. It features 64.0 GB of memory, providing a 2.0 GB per core ratio. The instance includes 1900 GB of local NVMe SSD storage and runs on the Nitro hypervisor. Network performance is anchored by a 15 Gbps baseline bandwidth.

Benchmark results show top-tier memory performance, with large-block read-only bandwidth reaching 384.64 GB/sec and write bandwidth at 170.56 GB/sec. Multi-core performance is highly competitive, as evidenced by a top-tier Geekbench multi-core score of 21489.0 and strong software compilation performance. Database operations are a notable strength, scoring in the top tier for Passmark database operations and demonstrating strong Redis SET performance at 70.72 million operations per second. However, large-scale LLM inference is a relative bottleneck, with prompt processing for a 70B model falling into the bottom 25% at 5.91 tokens per second.

Given its ARM64 architecture and high resource density, the server offers qualitative cost efficiency for multi-threaded workloads that benefit from dedicated physical cores without hyperthreading. The inclusion of 1900 GB of local NVMe SSD storage makes it highly suitable for high-throughput database operations, software compilation, static web serving, and multi-threaded decompression tasks. It is less suited for large-scale LLM inference workloads that require specialized accelerators.

Benchmark data highlights top-tier memory bandwidth, with large-block read-only speeds reaching 384.64 GB/sec, alongside top-tier multi-core performance in Geekbench and Passmark database operations. The server demonstrates strong capabilities in software compilation, Redis operations, and static web serving. While highly efficient for multi-threaded processing and database workloads due to its dedicated core topology and fast local storage, it exhibits lower performance in large-scale LLM inference. It represents a resource-dense option for high-throughput, non-GPU workloads.
